author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars’s apparent sky path during a retrograde episode: normal eastward drift, slowing to a stationary point, westward loop, second stationary point, and return to eastward drift.
Explain apparent retrograde motion in the heliocentric model as Earth overtaking a slower outer planet on an inner, faster orbit.
Contrast the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation and justify why the heliocentric model is preferred for simplicity and predictive power.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for an outer planet by identifying near-opposition geometry, with Earth between the Sun and the planet.
Compare Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn retrograde loops and explain why the apparent loop size decreases for more distant planets.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Mars Reverses Against the Stars
modules.description: A night-sky observing scene shows Mars moving against labeled ecliptic constellations over a simulated six-month retrograde episode.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify eastward prograde motion, stationary points, and westward retrograde motion in Mars’s apparent sky path.
Use constellation labels as fixed reference points for apparent planetary motion.
Describe why the observed loop was historically puzzling.
instructions: Face the curved starfield and read the constellation labels from left to right.
Advance through the clips and watch the red Mars point relative to the fixed stars.
Use the trail to reconstruct the full six-month apparent path.

components.text: Leo        Virgo        Libra        Scorpius
Start: Mars near Leo
Start: Mars near Leo

clips.changeMeaning: The opening view places Mars on the left side of a labeled ecliptic starfield so students can use the stars as fixed reference points.
clips.narration: We begin from Earth, the way early astronomers observed Mars: night after night against the distant stars of the ecliptic.

components.text: Months 1–2: eastward prograde drift

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves eastward and a short trail appears, emphasizing that planets usually drift east relative to the background stars.
clips.narration: For the first two months, Mars drifts slowly eastward. This normal apparent motion is called prograde motion.

components.text: Months 3–4: apparent westward retrograde loop

clips.changeMeaning: Mars shifts back westward while the trail expands into a loop, showing the temporary reversal and the approximate fifteen-degree angular extent.
clips.narration: Then Mars slows, appears to stop, and moves westward for about two months. The loop spans roughly fifteen degrees in the sky.

components.text: Months 5–6: eastward motion resumes

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves east of the loop and the complete trail remains visible, presenting the full observed pattern that demanded explanation.
clips.narration: Finally Mars stops again and resumes eastward motion. The historical puzzle was simple but profound: why would a planet appear to move backward?

modules.description: A tabletop geocentric model places Earth at the center while Mars rides on an epicycle carried by a deferent, reproducing retrograde motion through nested circles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define deferent and epicycle in the geocentric model.
Explain how nested circular motion can make Mars appear to reverse direction from Earth.
Evaluate the increasing complexity required by epicycle-based explanations.
instructions: Look down at the tabletop model with Earth in the center.
Follow Mars on the small epicycle while the epicycle center rides the larger deferent.
Notice the labeled inner part of the epicycle, where apparent backward motion occurs.

components.text: Geocentric model: Mars on an epicycle riding a deferent
Deferent = large circle; epicycle = small circle carrying Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The geocentric model appears with Earth, the deferent, the epicycle, and Mars separated clearly so the parts can be named before motion is implied.
clips.narration: In the geocentric picture, Earth sits at the center. Mars is attached to a small circle, the epicycle, whose center moves on a larger circle, the deferent.

components.text: Two circular motions combine into a loop-like apparent path

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle ring and Mars move to a new location on the deferent, demonstrating that Mars’s apparent path comes from two combined circular motions.
clips.narration: As the epicycle center moves around Earth, Mars also moves around the epicycle. The combination can be tuned to match the observed loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed on the Earth-facing side of the epicycle and the red arrow becomes visible, marking where the geocentric model produces apparent backward motion.
clips.narration: When Mars is on the inner side of the epicycle, closest to Earth, its combined motion can point opposite the usual eastward drift.

components.text: Fits the loop, but requires tuned epicycles for each planet

clips.changeMeaning: The label changes to emphasize that although epicycles can reproduce observations, the explanation becomes increasingly tuned and less parsimonious.
clips.narration: The model can reproduce retrograde motion, but each planet needs carefully adjusted sizes and speeds. Better data required more added circles, reducing simplicity.

modules.description: A top-down heliocentric model shows Earth and Mars moving on smooth orbits with Earth overtaking Mars on the inside track.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the relative orbital distances and periods of Earth and Mars.
Explain how Earth’s faster inner orbit produces retrograde episodes roughly every 26 months.
Recognize that Mars does not physically loop backward in the heliocentric model.
instructions: View the Sun-centered model from above the orbital plane.
Compare Earth’s smaller orbit with Mars’s larger orbit.
Advance the scene to see Earth catch and pass Mars.

components.text: Earth: 1 AU, 1 year     Mars: 1.52 AU, 1.88 years
Sun-centered view: two smooth orbits, no epicycle

clips.changeMeaning: The Sun-centered model appears with Earth and Mars on separate orbit rings, replacing the geocentric machinery with a simpler orbital layout.
clips.narration: In the heliocentric model, the Sun is central and both Earth and Mars move on smooth orbits around it.

components.text: Earth moves faster on the inner track

clips.changeMeaning: Earth advances farther along its smaller orbit than Mars advances on the outer orbit, making the relative speed difference visually explicit.
clips.narration: Earth is closer to the Sun and completes one orbit each year. Mars is farther out and takes about 1.88 years, so Earth moves faster.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars are placed near opposition with a visible alignment marker, identifying the geometry that corresponds to the retrograde episode.
clips.narration: About every twenty-six months, Earth catches up to Mars and passes it on the inside track, like a faster car passing a slower car.

components.text: The physical orbits stay smooth; the loop is apparent

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is shown after passing Mars while Mars remains on the smooth outer orbit, emphasizing that no physical backward loop or epicycle is required.
clips.narration: From outside the solar system, Mars never loops backward. The apparent loop appears only from Earth's changing viewpoint.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Line of Sight Connects Orbit to Sky
modules.description: A split view projects the line of sight from Earth through Mars onto a starfield, linking smooth heliocentric motion to the apparent retrograde loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace a line of sight from Earth through Mars to a background starfield.
Explain why the projected apparent position reverses during Earth’s overtaking of Mars.
Distinguish apparent geometric motion from an optical illusion or observational error.
instructions: Compare the heliocentric model on the left with the sky projection panel on the right.
Follow the yellow line from Earth through Mars.
Watch the projected Mars dot reverse when Earth overtakes Mars.

components.text: Line of sight maps heliocentric geometry to sky position

clips.changeMeaning: The split view introduces the line of sight and the projected Mars dot so students can connect the physical model to the apparent sky view.
clips.narration: Draw a line from Earth through Mars and extend it to the distant stars. Where the line meets the starfield is where Mars appears.

clips.changeMeaning: Before overtaking, the line and projected dot move eastward together, matching the normal prograde motion from the observation scene.
clips.narration: Before Earth catches Mars, the line of sight sweeps eastward through the constellations, so Mars appears to drift normally.

clips.changeMeaning: During overtaking, the line rotates the other way and the projected dot moves back westward, visibly tying the reversal to geometry.
clips.narration: As Earth overtakes Mars, the line of sight reverses its sweep. In the sky panel, Mars appears to retrace its path westward.

components.text: The loop is apparent, geometric, and observable

clips.changeMeaning: After the pass, the line and projected dot resume eastward motion, completing the east-west-east pattern through line-of-sight geometry.
clips.narration: After Earth has passed Mars, the line resumes its eastward sweep. Retrograde motion is a real apparent motion caused by changing viewpoint.

modules.description: Students walk around a floor circle representing Earth’s orbit while viewing Mars against distant stars, producing the retrograde effect through their own motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience how a moving viewpoint changes an object’s apparent position against a distant background.
Connect closest approach on an inner orbit with apparent reversal against the stars.
Explain retrograde motion using an embodied overtaking analogy.
instructions: Stand near the green footprint marker on the floor orbit.
Walk slowly clockwise while keeping Mars in view against the star wall.
Pause at the yellow closest-approach marker and note the reversal cue.

components.text: Walk the inner orbit; keep Mars aligned with the stars
Start at the green marker and face Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The walking orbit, start marker, Mars, and distant star wall appear to stage a safe embodied parallax activity in the user’s workspace.
clips.narration: In this scene, your body becomes Earth. Walk the small orbit while Mars stays beyond you against the distant stars.

components.text: Notice Mars drifting against the distant star wall

clips.changeMeaning: The arrow appears in the initial apparent drift direction and the instruction label cues students to begin walking around the inner orbit.
clips.narration: Begin walking slowly. As your viewpoint changes, Mars shifts against the background stars even though Mars itself has not jumped sideways.

components.text: Closest approach: apparent motion reverses

clips.changeMeaning: The closest-approach marker brightens and the arrow flips direction, connecting the student’s own inside-track pass to apparent backward motion.
clips.narration: Near closest approach, you pass Mars from the inside track. This is when the apparent shift reverses direction—the embodied version of retrograde motion.

components.text: You produced retrograde by overtaking on the inside track

clips.changeMeaning: The reversal cue softens and the label summarizes that the student’s moving viewpoint created the apparent retrograde effect.
clips.narration: After passing closest approach, the apparent motion returns to normal. Your changing viewpoint generated the retrograde pattern.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: A heliocentric comparison scene shows that Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn all retrograde, but their apparent loops shrink with distance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare approximate retrograde loop sizes for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain why Earth’s orbital motion subtends a smaller angle for more distant planets.
Apply parallax-style reasoning to outer-planet retrograde motion.
instructions: Observe the compressed but ordered distances of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Advance through each highlighted planet and compare the loop-size panel.
Relate the loop size to the planet’s distance from Earth and the Sun.

components.text: Retrograde loop size comparison
Compare loop sizes: Mars, Jupiter, Saturn

clips.changeMeaning: Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn appear in a compressed heliocentric layout with a loop panel ready for side-by-side comparison.
clips.narration: Mars is not unique. All outer planets can show retrograde motion, but the apparent loop size depends on distance.

components.text: Mars: about 15° across

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is highlighted and the panel shows the largest loop, representing the stronger angular shift for the closest of the three planets.
clips.narration: Mars is comparatively near, so Earth’s viewpoint shift is large. Mars can show a loop about fifteen degrees across.

components.text: Jupiter: about 10° across

clips.changeMeaning: Jupiter is highlighted and the displayed loop shrinks, showing that a more distant planet has a smaller apparent retrograde loop.
clips.narration: Jupiter is much farther away, near 5.2 astronomical units from the Sun. The same Earth motion makes a smaller loop, about ten degrees.

components.text: Saturn: about 7° across

clips.changeMeaning: Saturn is highlighted and the loop shrinks again, reinforcing the inverse relationship between distance and apparent angular shift.
clips.narration: Saturn is farther still, near 9.5 astronomical units, so its loop is smaller—about seven degrees in this comparison.

components.text: Greater distance → smaller apparent loop

clips.changeMeaning: The label summarizes the parallax principle, connecting the three loop sizes to the angular size of Earth’s orbit as seen from each planet.
clips.narration: This is parallax-style geometry: nearby objects shift more when your viewpoint moves, while distant objects shift less.

modules.description: Students place Mars around its orbit to predict where retrograde occurs, using a sky inset to confirm near-opposition geometry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict that retrograde for Mars occurs near opposition, when Earth is between the Sun and Mars.
Use relative Sun-Earth-Mars geometry rather than absolute direction to identify retrograde configurations.
Transfer the prediction to a second Earth position.
instructions: Drag or mentally place Mars on its orbit where retrograde should occur.
Use the yellow opposition arc as a hint when it appears.
Repeat after Earth moves to a new position and explain what stayed the same geometrically.

components.text: Prediction: where should Mars be for retrograde?
Place Mars where Earth is about to overtake it

clips.changeMeaning: The prediction scene begins with Earth fixed and Mars away from opposition, leaving the feedback inset blank so students can make an initial prediction.
clips.narration: Now predict the geometry. Where should Mars be for an observer on Earth to see retrograde motion?

components.text: Hint: align Sun–Earth–Mars with Earth in the middle

clips.changeMeaning: The opposition arc appears beyond Earth from the Sun, giving a visual hint that the correct location is near Sun-Earth-Mars alignment.
clips.narration: Hint: retrograde happens near opposition, when Earth lies between the Sun and the outer planet.

components.text: Correct: near opposition produces retrograde

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved to the near-opposition arc and the inset retrograde loop appears, confirming the predicted overtaking configuration.
clips.narration: Correct. With Mars near opposition, Earth is on the inside track and ready to overtake it, so the inset shows a retrograde loop.

components.text: Try again: find the new opposition direction

clips.changeMeaning: Earth moves to a new orbital position and Mars resets, showing that the correct retrograde region rotates with the Earth-Sun line.
clips.narration: Now Earth is elsewhere in its orbit. The absolute direction changed, but the relative geometry rule stays the same.

components.text: Correct again: relative geometry predicts the event

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves to the second correct near-opposition location and the feedback loop returns, reinforcing that relative alignment predicts retrograde.
clips.narration: Again, the correct configuration places Mars beyond Earth along the Sun-Earth line. Retrograde is predicted by relative geometry.

modules.description: A closing summary board highlights the observed phenomenon, geocentric epicycles, heliocentric overtaking, line-of-sight geometry, and planet-distance comparison.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the major conceptual steps in explaining apparent retrograde motion.
State a concise explanation using Earth overtaking Mars and changing line of sight.
Connect the historical model shift to parsimony and predictive success.
instructions: Read each highlighted recap item as the narrator reviews it.
At the final prompt, practice a one-sentence explanation using the word “overtake.”
Use the recap to connect observation, model, and prediction.

components.text: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Recap

1. Observed sky loop: east → west → east
2. Geocentric epicycles: workable but complex
3. Heliocentric model: Earth overtakes Mars
4. Line of sight projects smooth orbits into apparent loops
5. Farther planets make smaller loops
Final prompt: Explain retrograde motion using “Earth overtakes Mars.”

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight begins near the first recap line, returning students to the observed east-west-east sky pattern before reviewing explanations.
clips.narration: First, we observed the phenomenon: Mars drifts eastward, loops westward during retrograde, and then resumes eastward motion.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves downward to the model explanation lines, contrasting tuned epicycles with the simpler Sun-centered overtaking explanation.
clips.narration: The geocentric model used epicycles to fit the loop. The heliocentric model explains it more simply: Earth overtakes Mars on the inner orbit.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight expands over the line-of-sight and planet comparison lines, connecting apparent loops to projection geometry and planet distance.
clips.narration: The changing line of sight maps smooth orbits into an apparent sky loop. More distant planets shift less, so Jupiter and Saturn have smaller loops than Mars.

components.text: Your turn: Mars retrogrades because Earth overtakes Mars and the line of sight reverses.

clips.changeMeaning: The final prompt brightens and asks students to state the explanation in their own words, consolidating the core overtaking mechanism.
clips.narration: A concise explanation is: Mars appears to move backward when Earth overtakes it, changing our line of sight against distant stars. Now try saying it yourself.
